items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite being), mid-sentence blank; right subject is a component of the obvious noun
items.passage: The Lycurgus Cup, a fourth-century Roman glass vessel, looks opaque green in reflected light but translucent red when illuminated from behind. Despite being less than a ten-thousandth of a millimeter across, ______ responsible for this transformation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Lycurgus Cup contains particles of gold and silver that are
particles of gold and silver dispersed in the cup’s glass are
the cup’s glass holds particles of gold and silver, which are
there are particles of gold and silver in the cup’s glass that are
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something less than a ten-thousandth of a millimeter across, which can only be the tiny particles, not the cup or its glass. Choice B places “particles of gold and silver dispersed in the cup’s glass” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the particles.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
A.why_wrong: “The Lycurgus Cup” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the whole cup is less than a ten-thousandth of a millimeter across.

C.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
C.why_wrong: The head of “the cup’s glass” is “glass,” so the sentence says the cup’s glass, rather than the particles in it, is less than a ten-thousandth of a millimeter across.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: materials science and Roman history (dichroic glass, nanoparticles); invented nothing, no named researchers. Band 7 on the 37e5c794 (3.16) pattern with a component key: the size phrase admits only the particles; options 11 to 13 words, key not the longest; particles appear only in the options.
band7_moves: opener states a size that only a component of the obvious noun can have, so the right subject is the particles in the cup, not the cup (property or component key, as 2dd1b8bf and 3.27)
hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, failing only on what the phrase can describe
a possessive option starting with the cup (the cup’s glass) so the possessive form does not give the key away
mid-sentence blank with options ending in a verb or relative pronoun that must join the rest of the sentence, as in 37e5c794
key does not echo the passage: particles are named only in the options

band7.why: Component key on the 37e5c794 pattern: the size phrase fits only the particles, while the hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun, the cup, and keeps every fact, and C’s possessive also starts with the cup, so form does not point to the key. Every option is a grammatical clause; the only fault is what the opener describes. Key noun absent from the passage.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Calculated from), passage-final clause; right subject is a property (a trajectory)
items.passage: In February 2021, a brilliant fireball streaked across the night sky over England, and fragments of the meteorite responsible were recovered the following morning from a driveway in the town of Winchcombe. Calculated from footage captured by meteor-tracking cameras and household doorbell cameras, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the meteorite turned out to have come from the outer part of the asteroid belt.
the meteorite’s fragments revealed that it had come from the outer part of the asteroid belt.
it was the outer part of the asteroid belt that the meteorite had come from.
the fireball’s trajectory pointed back to the outer part of the asteroid belt.
items.explanation: Only a quantity such as a path or a trajectory can be calculated from camera footage. Choice D places “the fireball’s trajectory” right after the opening phrase, so the sentence correctly says the trajectory was calculated from the footage.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
A.why_wrong: “The meteorite” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the meteorite itself was calculated from footage.

B.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
B.why_wrong: The head of “the meteorite’s fragments” is “fragments,” so the sentence says the fragments, physical rocks found on a driveway, were calculated from footage.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: planetary science (Winchcombe meteorite, 2021). No named researchers. Band 7 on the fced396a / 3.27 pattern: “Calculated from footage” admits only a computed quantity, so the key’s head is a property (trajectory) while A and B start with the obvious noun; options 13 to 16 words, key not the longest.
band7_moves: opener predicate (Calculated from footage) can describe only a computed property, so the right subject is the fireball’s trajectory, not the meteorite (as “that of” forces the HHI score in fced396a and “Supported by” forces findings in 3.27)
hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact
possessive distractor built on the obvious noun (the meteorite’s fragments), so a possessive is not itself the cue
options 13 to 16 words, all grammatical as clauses; recipes W, P, E

band7.why: Property key as in fced396a and 8b017d4e: only a computed quantity (the trajectory) can be “calculated from footage,” while A and B start with the obvious noun, the meteorite, and A keeps every fact; key is the shortest option and its noun is absent from the passage. Weakest point: D alone drops “come from,” though it states the same fact.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final clause
items.passage: Fire ants native to the seasonally flooded wetlands of South America have an unusual strategy for surviving inundations that destroy their underground nests. Gripping one another with their mandibles and legs, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: thousands of workers form a raft that can float for days, sheltering the queen at its center.
a raft made of thousands of workers can float for days, sheltering the queen at its center.
the colony’s survival depends on thousands of workers linking together into a raft that can float for days.
it is a raft of thousands of linked workers that floats for days, sheltering the queen at its center.
items.explanation: The ants themselves are what grip one another with their mandibles and legs. Choice A places “thousands of workers” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the worker ants.

B.why_wrong: “A raft” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the raft grips one another with mandibles and legs.

C.why_wrong: The head of “the colony’s survival” is “survival,” so the sentence says the survival grips one another with mandibles and legs.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (fire ant rafts). Band 6: plain agent subject, recipes W, P, E; “one another” and “their mandibles” need a plural set of animals, which only A supplies. Key not the longest.

band7.why: Plain agent key (the workers) with W, P and E distractors, the band-6 shape (9 of 11 band-6 R3 keys are plain agents); band_target 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a long intervener of singular nouns with its own singular verb
items.passage: The self-portraits in Hong Kong–born photographer Tseng Kwong Chi’s East Meets West series, in which the artist poses stiffly in a Mao suit before a landmark such as Mount Rushmore, ______ simultaneously humorous and unsettling, since the solemn figure in each could be either a tourist or a visiting official.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “self-portraits”; everything from “in Hong Kong–born” to “Mount Rushmore” describes them. The plural verb “are” agrees with “self-portraits.”

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular, so it does not agree with the plural subject “self-portraits”; it matches the nearer nouns “series” and “Mount Rushmore.”

B.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and does not agree with “self-portraits.”

D.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and does not agree with “self-portraits.”

items.notes: Subject: photography (Tseng Kwong Chi, East Meets West). Band-7 settings: plural head behind 23 words of singular nouns (photographer, series, artist, suit, landmark, Mount Rushmore); the intervener has its own singular verb (“poses”), so the singular reads right twice; 18 words follow the blank; run 48 words.
band7_moves: plural head (self-portraits) behind singular nouns, as b32eab9f and 3.3
intervener contains a relative clause whose own verb agrees with the singular attractor (in which the artist poses), as 0fe5ce68 and 1c65db8f
five singular attractors between head and blank; “series” sits right before the clause and makes “is” sound right
run of 48 words with 18 after the blank

band7.why: Plural head (self-portraits) behind singular nouns only (photographer, series, artist, suit, landmark, Mount Rushmore) and a relative clause with its own singular verb (poses), as 8a9d2f4e and 0fe5ce68; 18 words follow the blank and all three distractors are singular, so the nearest-noun reading sounds right twice.

fixes: trimmed “and mirrored sunglasses” (54 to 51 words; transcript models 57 and 59, band-7 officials 45 and 57); this also removes the only plural noun inside the intervener, so every noun between head and blank is singular
word_count recounted with check_rw.words(): 53 to 51

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb delayed by a dash interrupter that contains its own finite verb
items.passage: Oral rehydration solution—water mixed with precisely measured amounts of salt and glucose, which together enable the intestine to absorb fluid—______ millions of lives since doctors first used it widely in refugee camps during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “Oral rehydration solution”; the dashes only set off a description of the solution. “Has saved” is a finite verb that agrees with the singular subject and fits “since,” so it completes the sentence.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: “Saving” cannot serve as the sentence’s main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having saved” is a participle and leaves the sentence without a main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: “To save” is an infinitive and leaves the sentence without a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: medicine and history (oral rehydration therapy, 1971 refugee camps). No named people. Band 6 as 3.13: the dash interrupter holds its own finite verb (“enable”), so a reader may think the main clause already has its verb; 18 words between subject and blank.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a sound band 6 on the 3.13 pattern (dash interrupter holding its own verb, 18 words between subject and blank).

items.subtype: Possessive determiner: plural antecedent 17 words before the blank, singular nouns between
items.passage: An Eciton burchellii army ant colony builds no permanent nest. During its nomadic phase, the colony relocates almost nightly, and wherever it halts, hundreds of thousands of workers assemble a temporary shelter, known as a bivouac, around the queen and her brood by interlocking ______ legs and mandibles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The legs and mandibles belong to the “workers,” a plural noun, so the plural possessive determiner “their” is needed.

A.recipe: contraction for possessive determiner, wrong number
A.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is,” which makes no sense before “legs,” and it is singular.

B.why_wrong: “They’re” means “they are,” which makes no sense before “legs.”

C.why_wrong: “Its” is singular, so it cannot refer to the plural “workers”; it matches the nearer singular nouns “shelter,” “bivouac,” “queen,” and “brood” and the earlier “colony.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (army ant bivouacs). Band 6 as 2cb1ee22: antecedent 16 words back with singular nouns between (shelter, bivouac, queen, brood); the singular “colony” and the passage’s own “its nomadic phase” make “its” tempting; contractions are the easy rejects.

band7.why: Antecedent 16 words back with only singular nouns between (after the fix) and “its” tempted by the colony; band-7 R5 settings (determiner before its antecedent, as 0bcb4417) not used; band_target 6 as planned.

fixes: “the queen and larvae” became “the queen and her brood”: the plural “larvae” right before the blank pointed to “their”; now only singular nouns stand between “workers” and the blank (hardened through the rule)

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate, split from the first by a long object and a dash interrupter
items.passage: British engineer Hertha Ayrton attributed the persistent hissing of electric arc lamps, then common in street lighting, to oxygen reaching the lamps’ incandescent carbon electrodes—a discovery she reported in 1899—and ______ that same year the first woman elected to the Institution of Electrical Engineers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “And” joins a second action to the subject “Hertha Ayrton,” whose first verb is “attributed.” The past tense finite verb “became” matches “attributed” and gives the second half of the compound predicate a main verb.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: “Becoming” is not a finite verb, so it cannot pair with “attributed” as the second verb of the predicate.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: “To become” is an infinitive and cannot serve as the second main verb joined to “attributed.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having become” is a participle and cannot serve as the second main verb joined to “attributed.”

items.notes: Subject: history of engineering (Hertha Ayrton, arc lamps). No band-7 official items exist for R2_finite_second (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md), so the plan’s band 7 is written as a strong band 6 and band_target set to 6. 30 words between the first verb and the blank, with a dash interrupter holding its own finite verb (“reported”), as in 2.1.

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), so it cannot be band 7; left a strong band 6: 30 words and a dash interrupter with its own verb between “attributed” and the blank, as 2.1.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a relative-clause intervener holding plural nouns
items.passage: Beginning in 2000, India built paved roads to thousands of isolated villages. A 2020 study, which compared villages that received the new roads with similar villages that did not, ______ the assumption that rural roads primarily help farmers market their crops: the roads mainly moved workers out of agriculture and into wage employment.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “study”; the clause “which compared villages that received the new roads with similar villages that did not” only describes it. The singular verb “challenges” agrees with “study.”

A.why_wrong: “Challenge” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “study”; it matches the nearer plural noun “villages.”

B.why_wrong: “Are challenging” is plural and does not agree with “study.”

D.why_wrong: “Have challenged” is plural and does not agree with “study.”

items.notes: Subject: economics (India’s rural road program; the 2020 regression-discontinuity study by Asher and Novosad, researchers unnamed). Reviewer replaced the writer’s 2019 lost-wallet study, a widely reported subject. Medium: 14-word relative clause with three plural nouns (villages, roads, villages) between head and blank; its own verbs (received, did) show no number.

fixes: subject replaced: the 2019 lost-wallet study (17,000 wallets, 40 countries) is a front-page, widely reported study, a topic-fame tell; now India’s rural road program and its 2020 evaluation (researchers unnamed), same frame: singular “study” + relative clause with plural nouns + blank; all four options retested in the full sentence, only “challenges” agrees; claimed in claims.txt
word_count recounted with check_rw.words(): 51 to 52

items.subtype: Personal pronoun with its verb: singular antecedent, plural nouns and a named person nearer the blank
items.passage: In 1756, German physician Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost described what happens when a drop of water lands on an iron spoon heated in a fire to temperatures far above the boiling point. Rather than evaporating immediately, ______ across the spoon’s surface, insulated from the scorching metal by a thin cushion of vapor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: What skitters across the spoon is “a drop of water,” a singular noun, so the singular pronoun and verb “it skitters” are needed.

B.why_wrong: “They” is plural and cannot refer to the singular “drop”; the nearer plural noun “temperatures” cannot skitter across a spoon.

C.recipe: wrong referent (the person named in the passage)
C.why_wrong: “He” could only refer to Leidenfrost, who did not skitter across the spoon.

D.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and cannot refer to the singular “drop.”

items.notes: Subject: physics (the Leidenfrost effect, 1756). Medium as 2.15 and 2.3: the singular antecedent sits in the previous sentence, a plural noun (temperatures) and a named man (Leidenfrost) are planted as rivals; options carry the verb so number shows twice, as in 2.4.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After appearing), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Senegalese director Safi Faye was the first woman from sub-Saharan Africa to make a commercially distributed feature film. After appearing as an actor in a film by French ethnographer Jean Rouch, ______ an intimate portrait of farm life in her native village.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Faye’s first feature was Kaddu Beykat (1975),
Kaddu Beykat (1975) was the first feature Faye made,
it was Faye who made Kaddu Beykat (1975),
items.explanation: Faye is the person who appeared as an actor in a film by Jean Rouch. Choice D places “Faye” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes her.

A.why_wrong: The head of “Faye’s first feature” is “feature,” so the sentence illogically says a film appeared as an actor in Rouch’s film.

B.why_wrong: “Kaddu Beykat (1975)” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the film itself appeared as an actor in Rouch’s film.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: film (Safi Faye). Medium: short opener, plain person key, recipes P, W, E; key the shortest option.

fixes: subtype said “After working”; the passage opens “After appearing”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head, relative clause with singular nouns before the blank
items.passage: The chalk cliffs that rise above the English Channel near the port of Dover ______ composed primarily of coccoliths, microscopic plates of calcium carbonate shed by single-celled algae that flourished in a warm sea covering much of northern Europe approximately 70 to 100 million years ago.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun “cliffs”; the clause “that rise above ... Dover” describes them. The plural verb “are” agrees with “cliffs.”

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and does not agree with “cliffs”; it matches the nearer nouns “port” and “Dover.”

C.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and does not agree with “cliffs.”

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and does not agree with “cliffs.”

items.notes: Subject: geology (chalk of the Dover cliffs, coccoliths). Medium: 12 words between head and blank, with three singular nouns (Channel, port, Dover).

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Composed of), mid-sentence blank; key starts with a possessive
items.passage: In 1886, nineteen-year-old Rubén Darío left his native Nicaragua for Chile, where he found work as a journalist. Composed of short prose narratives and a handful of poems, ______ is often credited with launching modernismo, a movement that renewed Spanish-language literature.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Darío, who published the book Azul there in 1888,
the appearance of Darío’s Azul in 1888
it is Darío’s Azul, published there in 1888, that
items.explanation: Only a book can be composed of prose narratives and poems. In choice C the subject is “Darío’s Azul,” whose head noun is the book “Azul,” so the opening phrase correctly describes the book.

A.why_wrong: “Darío” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the writer himself was composed of prose narratives and poems.

B.why_wrong: The head of “the appearance of Darío’s Azul” is “appearance,” so the sentence says an appearance, an event, was composed of narratives and poems.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Rubén Darío, Azul, 1888). Medium as 2.19: the key is a possessive noun phrase whose head is the thing described, so a student who rejects every possessive misses it.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing result phrase after a complete clause and a comma
items.passage: From the 1970s onward, the Brazilian television network Globo extended its signal across the country, bringing its telenovelas into millions of homes. Women in newly reached areas later had fewer children, ______ researchers to link the decline to the small, prosperous families portrayed in the shows.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause before the comma is already complete, with the subject “Women” and the verb “had.” The participle “prompting” begins a phrase that describes a result of that clause without adding a second main verb.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: “Prompted” adds a second main verb after a complete clause with no conjunction or subject, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: “Was prompting” is a finite verb with no subject or conjunction, joined to a complete clause by only a comma.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Prompts” is a finite verb with no subject or conjunction, joined to a complete clause by only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science (television and fertility in Brazil). Researchers unnamed. Medium as 2.9: result phrase after a long complete clause.

fixes: trimmed “prime-time” (47 to 45 words) as the writer asked; by check_rw’s count it was already below its models (2.9: 55, 1.29: 48)
word_count recounted with check_rw.words(): 47 to 45

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a short subject
items.passage: Each morning in Tamil Nadu, India, many women create kolam, decorative drawings, outside the entrances of their households. A kolam ______ of rice-flour lines that curve around a carefully spaced grid of dots, forming a symmetrical pattern.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “A kolam.” “Consists” is a finite verb that agrees with the singular subject, so it completes the sentence.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: “Consisting” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
B.why_wrong: “Having consisted” leaves the sentence without a main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: “To consist” leaves the sentence without a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: culture and design (kolam drawings in Tamil Nadu). Easy: subject right before the blank.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun (object): singular antecedent, no rival noun
items.passage: A Mexican jumping bean is the seed of a shrub native to northern Mexico, with the larva of a small moth developing inside. When sunlight warms the seed, the larva contracts its body vigorously, causing ______ to roll and hop unpredictably across the ground.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: What rolls and hops is “the seed,” a singular noun, so the singular pronoun “it” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Them” is plural and cannot refer to the singular “seed.”

C.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and cannot refer to the singular “seed.”

D.why_wrong: “These” is plural and cannot refer to the singular “seed.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Mexican jumping beans). Easy: singular antecedent in the same sentence, every distractor plural.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun (subject): a named person as antecedent
items.passage: In 1920, vocalist Mamie Smith recorded “Crazy Blues” for Okeh Records in New York City, becoming the first Black singer to release a blues recording. The record sold remarkably well, and ______ soon embarked on an extensive national tour with her band, the Jazz Hounds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who embarked on a tour with “her band” is Mamie Smith, so the singular pronoun “she” is needed.

B.why_wrong: “They” is plural, but the antecedent, Mamie Smith, is one person.

C.why_wrong: “It” would refer to the record, and a record cannot go on tour with “her band.”

D.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and has no plural antecedent in the passage.

items.notes: Subject: music history (Mamie Smith, “Crazy Blues”). Easy as 1.33: the person named in the first sentence is the antecedent.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head right before the blank
items.passage: Cartographers on the Mediterranean island of Majorca were renowned in the 1300s for their exceptionally detailed navigational charts. The Catalan Atlas ______ produced there around 1375 and depicts coastlines, kingdoms, and trading cities from the Atlantic Ocean to China.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject, “The Catalan Atlas,” is singular, and the atlas was produced in the past, around 1375. The singular verb “was” agrees with the subject.

A.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “The Catalan Atlas.”

B.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and does not agree with “The Catalan Atlas.”

C.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and does not agree with “The Catalan Atlas.”

items.notes: Subject: history of cartography (the Catalan Atlas). Easy: no intervener; the plural “Cartographers” sits in the previous sentence only.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head right before the blank
items.passage: Chinese writer Xiao Hong completed her novel Tales of Hulan River in Hong Kong in 1940, far from the northeastern town where she grew up. The novel ______ that town through loosely connected vignettes of its residents, seasons, and festivals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject, “The novel,” is singular, so the singular verb “portrays” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: “Portray” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “The novel.”

C.why_wrong: “Are portraying” is plural and does not agree with “The novel.”

D.why_wrong: “Have portrayed” is plural and does not agree with “The novel.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Xiao Hong, Tales of Hulan River). Easy: subject right before the blank.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a yearly custom
items.passage: The Great Mosque of Djenné, in Mali, is the world’s largest mud-brick building, and seasonal rains erode part of its exterior every year. Each spring, before the rainy season returns, the town’s residents ______ the structure’s walls with a protective layer of fresh mud plaster.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Each spring” and the present tense verbs “is,” “erode,” and “returns” show that the passage describes something that happens regularly now. The simple present “coat” fits that time frame.

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Coated” places a yearly, ongoing custom in the past, which clashes with the present tense of the passage.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: “Had coated” refers to a time before some other past event, but the passage describes a present custom.

D.why_wrong: “Were coating” describes an action in progress at a past time, not a regular present custom.

items.notes: Subject: architecture and culture (annual replastering of the Great Mosque of Djenné). Easy: habitual cue “Each spring” plus present verbs in the same sentence.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a general fact
items.passage: Hellbenders, giant salamanders that inhabit fast-flowing streams in the eastern United States, absorb most of their oxygen directly through their skin. Wrinkled folds of skin along the animals’ sides ______ the surface area available for absorbing dissolved oxygen from the water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage states general facts about how hellbenders live, using the present tense (“inhabit,” “absorb”). The simple present “increase” fits that time frame.

A.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
A.why_wrong: “Had increased” refers to a time before another past event, but the passage describes a present, general fact.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession by two plural possessors, cue after the blank
items.passage: Golden moles, which inhabit southern Africa, and marsupial moles, which inhabit Australian deserts, last shared a common ancestor more than 100 million years ago. A.why_wrong: “Golden moles” and “marsupial moles” are plain plurals here; the context requires the plural possessives “golden moles’” and “marsupial moles’.”

D.recipe: joint possession where each group has its own (individual possession)
D.why_wrong: Putting the apostrophe only on the second noun suggests a single set of bodies shared by both groups, but the text describes each group’s bodies separately.

items.notes: Subject: golden moles and marsupial moles, convergent evolution (science, zoology). Band-7 setting: individual possession as in 4c335aea, here with generic plural possessors as in 2784cbaf (objects’); the deciding cue (“in each group”) comes 13 words after the blank. The bare plural (A) is offered and is wrong because a plural noun cannot modify another noun here (“marsupial moles bodies”); no singular attributive form (“marsupial mole bodies”) is offered, since that would be acceptable. Band-7 settings: the opener describes a part, not the animal the passage is about (the component key b1 used, here with a new opener, Before + -ing, and a passage-final blank as in 188f7e3c); the hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact; the key’s noun (sheath) is not in the passage, which says “outer covering.” Recipes W, W, E; the expletive is built on “new keratin,” not on the key’s noun. Weakest point: the first sentence names the thing that falls off (“outer covering”) before the opener, so a careful reader can match it to “sheath.” Reviewer: B was “new keratin grows ...,” killed at a glance by new versus old; it is now a nominalised subject that carries the key’s noun (the loosening of each horn’s old sheath), as 2bca654a’s “the transport of nutrients,” and the key is recast as an X’s Y subject (each horn’s old sheath). band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on a75d5984: 29 words from head to blank holding a relative clause, an infinitive and an -ing noun, with no comma marking the end of the subject.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner before its singular antecedent, plural nouns before and right after the blank
items.passage: In medieval Europe, fiddles were played with horsehair bows, as violins are today. With ______ strings set vibrating instead by a rosined wooden wheel that the performer rotates with a crank, the hurdy-gurdy, another instrument of that era, can sustain a continuous drone for as long as the wheel keeps revolving.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank comes before its antecedent: the phrase “With ______ strings set vibrating instead by a rosined wooden wheel ...” describes “the hurdy-gurdy,” the subject of the main clause. The singular possessive determiner “its” agrees with that singular noun.

A.recipe: contraction for possessive determiner, wrong number
A.why_wrong: “They’re” is a contraction of “they are,” not a possessive, and it is plural, while the strings belong to the singular “hurdy-gurdy.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “their” doesn’t agree with the singular “the hurdy-gurdy”; it can only point back to the fiddles, whose strings are played with bows, not with a wheel.

D.why_wrong: “It’s” is a contraction of “it is,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: the hurdy-gurdy (arts, music). Band-7 settings from 0bcb4417: the determiner comes 16 words before its antecedent, inside a fronted with-phrase (the possessed noun follows directly, as in the model, but the antecedent is singular, varying both models’ “their”); plural nouns sit before the blank (fiddles, bows, violins) and right after it (strings), so “their” is the nearest-noun trap, and the first sentence’s fiddles are logically excluded because their strings are bowed. The 2 x 2 grid (its, it’s, their, they’re).

band7.why: The 0bcb4417 setting: the determiner sits 16 words before its antecedent inside a fronted with-phrase, with plural nouns before (fiddles, bows, violins) and right after (strings) the blank, so “their” reads well until “the hurdy-gurdy” arrives; the 2 x 2 grid of both band-7 officials, with a singular antecedent varying their “their.”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject with a contrast tag (X and Y, not Z); every intervening verb and noun in the run singular; options as c7cb5186 (two singular forms, one nonfinite)
items.passage: In Croatia’s Plitvice Lakes, sixteen lakes descend a forested valley in a series of terraces, each held back by a natural barrier of porous travertine. The calcium carbonate that precipitates from the mineral-rich water, settling fastest wherever the current churns and splashes, and the moss that traps this mineral before it can wash downstream, not any ancient landslide, ______ these distinctive barriers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is compound: “The calcium carbonate that precipitates from the mineral-rich water ... and the moss that traps this mineral ...,” two things joined by “and.” The phrase “not any ancient landslide” is set off by commas and doesn’t change the subject’s number, so the blank needs a plural finite verb: “build.”

A.why_wrong: The singular verb “builds” agrees with the nearby “landslide” or with “moss,” not with the compound subject joined by “and.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “has built” doesn’t agree with the compound subject joined by “and.”

D.why_wrong: “Building” has no singular ending, but it isn’t a finite verb: with it, the compound subject never gets a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: Plitvice Lakes travertine barriers (science, geology). The reviewer replaced the first subject (why glacier ice looks blue): official Command of Evidence item 8545ccfe explains blue ice by the same bubble-free mechanism. Band-7 settings kept: a plural (compound) key behind singular nouns only (calcium carbonate, water, current, moss, mineral, landslide) and interveners with their own singular verbs (“precipitates,” “churns,” “splashes,” “traps”), as the band-7 recipe asks; the contrast tag as in c7cb5186 with each conjunct long; about 30 words from the first head to the blank; the first conjunct closes with a participial aside set off by a comma pair and ending on an intransitive verb (“splashes”), so no comma falls between the two halves of the subject and “the moss” cannot be misread as a second object of “from,” and the noun right before the blank (“landslide”) is singular. Option set as c7cb5186 (determines, determining, has determined, determine), so a student who settles the number still has two options and must check finiteness. The two compounds already in the bank (w1b4_06, the Bajau item) have no contrast tag. Plain geology, no named study.

fixes: subject replaced: why glacier ice looks blue is explained by the same bubble-free mechanism in official Command of Evidence item 8545ccfe; new passage on Plitvice travertine barriers with the same scaffold (compound subject, not-Z tag, singular nouns and verbs only in the run, register kept at CB’s hard figures)
hardened: “is producing” replaced by the nonfinite “building,” the c7cb5186 option set; explanation, rationales, notes and claims.txt updated

band7.why: c7cb5186’s design with longer conjuncts: compound subject with a not-Z tag, plural key behind singular nouns only, two intervener verbs of the other number (precipitates, churns, splashes, traps); after the fix the option set is c7cb5186’s (two singular finite forms and a nonfinite -ing), so number alone leaves two options and finiteness decides.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head behind a participial phrase holding plural nouns; lexical-verb options

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are describing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “term.”

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun with a singular antecedent a sentence back, plural rivals between
items.passage: At dusk, many parrotfish species spend up to an hour enclosing themselves in a cocoon of mucus secreted by glands in their gills. Blood-feeding parasites called gnathiid isopods attack reef fishes at night, and researchers in Australia found that ______ can shield sleeping parrotfish from these pests.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun must refer to the thing that shields the sleeping fish: the singular noun “cocoon” in the first sentence. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with “cocoon.”

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “cocoon”; the plural nouns nearby, such as “isopods” and “researchers,” can’t be what shields the fish.

C.recipe: right kind of slot, wrong number demonstrative
C.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “cocoon.”

D.why_wrong: “One” would refer to an unspecified person or thing, not back to the cocoon the passage describes.

items.notes: Subject: parrotfish mucus cocoons and gnathiid isopods (science, marine biology). Medium setting: antecedent one sentence back, with plural rivals between (parasites, isopods, fishes, researchers); the verb after the blank is a modal, so number shows only in the pronoun. Researchers left unnamed (the Lizard Island work).

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After + -ing), mid-sentence blank; the writer is the right subject
items.passage: After withdrawing from society to the quiet, forested hills surrounding Kyoto, then Japan’s capital, ______ a brief meditation on the impermanence of all things.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Hōjōki (1212) was written by Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei as
Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei wrote the Hōjōki (1212),
Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei’s Hōjōki (1212) was composed as
a hut is where Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei wrote the Hōjōki (1212),
items.explanation: Only a person can withdraw from society, so the noun right after the opening phrase must name the writer. Choice B places “Japanese poet Kamo no Chōmei” there, so the sentence correctly says that he withdrew and then wrote the Hōjōki.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “The Hōjōki” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the book withdrew from society.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “Hōjōki,” not Kamo no Chōmei, so the sentence illogically says that the book withdrew from society.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the place
D.why_wrong: “A hut” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the hut withdrew from society.

items.notes: Subject: Kamo no Chōmei’s Hōjōki (literature). Medium setting: a short, clear opener and a plain agent key, as in 2.17. Recipes V, P, W; no it-cleft wrapping the key. Key is the shortest option. Facts are standard (Hōjōki, 1212, written in a small hut in the hills around Kyoto); the reviewer made “southeast of Kyoto” general, since he first withdrew to Ōhara and only later moved to Hino.

fixes: “wooded hills southeast of Kyoto” made general (“forested hills surrounding Kyoto, then Japan’s capital”): Chōmei first withdrew to Ōhara, only later to Hino

items.subtype: Tense: simple past with a relative-time cue (“Some six centuries later”) and a past relative clause
items.passage: Carolingian minuscule, a legible, rounded script, spread through Europe’s monasteries in the late 700s and the 800s. Some six centuries later, Italian humanists who mistook manuscripts written in it for ancient Roman texts ______ a new script on its letterforms, which early printers later adapted for movable type.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes events of the early Renaissance: “Some six centuries later” counts forward from the 700s and 800s, and the other verbs (“mistook,” “adapted”) are in the past tense. The simple past “modeled” fits this past time frame.

C.recipe: present simple where past is needed
C.why_wrong: The present “model” doesn’t fit the past events the sentence describes.

items.notes: Subject: Carolingian minuscule and the humanist script (history). Medium setting: the time cue is relative (counted from the first sentence’s dates), with past verbs on both sides of the blank. No named humanist.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate split by a parenthesis
items.passage: Largely self-taught as a composer, American pianist Amy Beach learned orchestration by studying the scores of European masters. She then wrote her “Gaelic” Symphony (a work built on Irish folk melodies) and ______ it premiered by the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1896.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “And” joins two verbs that share the subject “She”: “wrote” and the verb in the blank. To match the finite past tense verb “wrote,” the blank needs the finite past tense verb “saw.”

B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to see” can’t serve as the second main verb after “wrote ... and.”

C.why_wrong: “Having seen” can’t serve as the second main verb after “wrote ... and.”

items.notes: Subject: Amy Beach’s Gaelic Symphony, premiered by the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1896 (arts, music). Medium setting from 2.1 (band 6 there): a compound predicate whose two verbs are split by an interrupter, here a parenthesis instead of 2.1’s dash pair.

items.passage: Not every volcano erupts molten rock. The mud volcanoes of Azerbaijan, for example, ______ a mixture of mud, water, and hydrocarbon gases such as methane, which occasionally ignites at the surface.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual action (“Each evening”), parallel with present verbs
items.passage: The prayer plant, a low-growing tropical herb native to Brazil’s rainforests, owes its name to a daily movement known as nyctinasty. Each evening, its leaves ______ upward and press together, resembling a pair of hands folded in prayer; at sunrise, they gradually unfold again.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes something the plant does every day: “Each evening” marks a repeated action, and the other verbs (“owes,” “press,” “unfold”) are in the present tense. The simple present “fold” fits this habitual action.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “folded” doesn’t fit a movement that still happens every evening, as “owes,” “press,” and “unfold” show.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had folded” places the action before some past moment, which doesn’t fit a present-day daily habit.

C.why_wrong: The past progressive “were folding” describes an action in progress in the past, not a repeated present one.

items.notes: Subject: the prayer plant’s night folding (science, botany). Easy setting: explicit habitual cue (“Each evening”) and a parallel present verb right after the blank, as in 1.17 and 1.3.

B.why_wrong: “Sanctuaries” is a plain plural rather than a possessive, and “step’s” is a possessive where a plain plural is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Sanctuaries’” is a plural possessive, but the statues were carved for a single sanctuary.

items.notes: Subject: Aleijadinho’s prophets at Congonhas (arts, sculpture). Number cue for the possessor: “a hilltop sanctuary.” Avoids the bank’s frequent “Many of the ______” frame. Facts are standard (twelve soapstone prophets, 1800 to 1805, Sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos).

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: American linguist Arnold Zwicky coined the term “recency illusion” in 2005 ______ a widespread misconception: the assumption that a linguistic usage one has only recently noticed must itself be a recent innovation.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “describes” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction or a subject of its own.

items.notes: Subject: Arnold Zwicky’s recency illusion (social science, linguistics). Canonical purpose-infinitive set (1.27: has studied, to study, studied, studies). Zwicky coined the term on Language Log in 2005.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action continuing up to a dated past event (“By then”)

C.why_wrong: The future “will use” doesn’t fit an action that had already gone on for two centuries by the 1020s.

items.notes: Subject: Tang flying cash before Song paper money (history). Easy setting from 1.24: the earlier past is fixed by an explicit cue (“By then” after a dated sentence). No simple past option, so the past perfect is the only defensible form.

items.notes: Subject: Singapore’s hawker centers (social science, urban policy). Option set as in 1.29 (ensuring, this will ensure, ensures, it ensures).
